chapters.title: Problema I — Is there a teleological suspension of the ethical?
paragraphs: The ethical as such is the universal. As the universal, it applies to everyone — which can also be put another way: it applies at every moment. It rests within itself. Nothing outside it is its telos (its end: the purpose it exists for); instead, it is itself the telos of everything outside it, and once the ethical has taken all of that into itself, it goes no further. The single individual — the individual person, defined as he immediately is, a being of senses and soul — is the single individual who has his telos in the universal. His ethical task is to express himself in the universal continually: to cancel his particularity (whatever sets him apart as this one person) in order to become the universal. As soon as the single individual tries to assert himself in his particularity against the universal, he sins, and only by acknowledging this can he be reconciled with the universal again. Whenever the single individual, after having entered the universal, feels an urge to assert himself as the single individual, he is in a spiritual trial — an inner assault he must resist — and he can work his way out of it only by repenting and giving himself up, as the single individual, in the universal. If this is the highest thing that can be said about a human being and his existence, then the ethical is of the same nature as a person's eternal blessedness, which for all eternity and at every moment is his telos. For it would be a contradiction if eternal blessedness could be given up — that is, teleologically suspended — since the moment it was suspended, it would be forfeited. What is teleologically suspended, by contrast, is not forfeited but is preserved precisely in the higher thing that is its telos.

If that is how things stand, then Hegel is right to define a human being under "the Good and Conscience" only as the single individual. He is right to regard this condition as a "moral form of evil" (see especially his Philosophy of Right), one that must be cancelled in the teleology of ethical life — the morality that is lived out in family, society and state. On this view, the single individual who remains at that stage either sins or is in a spiritual trial. Where Hegel is wrong, however, is in speaking of faith. He is wrong not to protest loudly and clearly against Abraham's enjoying honor and glory as a father of faith, when Abraham ought instead to be sent back to a lower court and exposed as a murderer.

For faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual is higher than the universal. But note carefully how this is so: the movement repeats itself. Having first been in the universal, the single individual now sets himself apart, as the single individual, as higher than the universal. If this is not faith, then Abraham is lost, and faith has never existed in the world — precisely because it has always existed. For suppose that the ethical — that is, ethical life — is the highest, and that nothing incommensurable remains in a human being (nothing that cannot be measured by that common standard) except in the sense that this incommensurable element is evil, namely the particular, which ought to be expressed in the universal. In that case one needs no categories beyond those Greek philosophy had, or those that consistent thinking can derive from them. Hegel should not have concealed this; after all, he had studied the Greeks.

One quite often hears men who, instead of losing themselves in study, lose themselves in phrases, announce that a light shines over the Christian world while darkness broods over paganism. This talk has always struck me as strange, since every more thorough thinker, every more serious artist, still renews himself in the eternal youth of the Greek people. Such a statement can be explained by the fact that people do not know what to say, only that they must say something. It is quite in order to say that paganism did not have faith. But if saying so is to mean anything, one must be a little clearer about what one understands by faith; otherwise one sinks back into phrases like these. It is easy to explain the whole of existence, faith included, without having any idea of what faith is. And the man who counts on being admired for such an explanation is not the worst calculator in life; for, as Boileau says, un sot trouve toujours un plus sot, qui l'admire — a fool always finds a bigger fool to admire him.

Faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — is justified over against it, not subordinate to it but above it. But note carefully how this is so: it is the single individual who, after having been subordinate to the universal as the single individual, now, through the universal, becomes the single individual who as the single individual stands above it. The single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute. This position cannot be mediated — that is, it cannot be settled by being brought under the universal and explained there — for all mediation takes place precisely by means of the universal. It is and remains for all eternity a paradox, inaccessible to thought. And yet either faith is this paradox, or else — these are the consequences I ask the reader to keep in mind at every point, even though it would become too long-winded for me to write them out everywhere — or else there has never been faith, precisely because it has always existed, or else Abraham is lost.

It is true that the single individual can easily mistake this paradox for a spiritual trial, but that is no reason to conceal it. It is true that many people may be so constituted that the paradox repels them. But that is no reason to turn faith into something else so that one can have it too; better to admit that one does not have it. And those who do have faith should take care to set out some marks by which one could tell the paradox apart from a spiritual trial.

Now, the story of Abraham contains just such a teleological suspension of the ethical. There has been no shortage of sharp minds and thorough scholars who have found analogies to it. Their wisdom comes down to the fine principle that basically everything is the same. If one looks a little more closely, I very much doubt that anyone will find a single analogy in the whole world — except a later one, which proves nothing if it stands firm that Abraham represents faith, and that faith finds its normal expression in him, whose life is not merely the most paradoxical that can be thought, but so paradoxical that it cannot be thought at all. He acts by virtue of the absurd; for the absurd is precisely this: that he as the single individual is higher than the universal. This paradox cannot be mediated. For as soon as Abraham begins to mediate it, he has to admit that he was in a spiritual trial; and if so, he never gets as far as sacrificing Isaac — or, if he has already sacrificed Isaac, he must return in repentance to the universal. By virtue of the absurd he gets Isaac back. Abraham is therefore at no moment a tragic hero; he is something altogether different — either a murderer or a believer. The middle term that saves the tragic hero is something Abraham does not have. That is why I can understand a tragic hero but cannot understand Abraham, even though in a certain mad sense I admire him more than anyone else.

Ethically expressed, Abraham's relation to Isaac is quite simply this: the father must love the son more than himself. But the ethical has several gradations within its own range. We shall see whether this story contains any higher expression of the ethical that could explain his conduct ethically — that could ethically justify him in suspending his ethical obligation to his son, without his thereby going beyond the teleology of the ethical, the ordering of purposes that lies within the ethical itself.

When an undertaking that concerns a whole people is thwarted, when such an enterprise is halted by heaven's disfavor, when the angry deity sends a dead calm that mocks every effort, when the seer carries out his heavy task and announces that the god demands a young girl as a sacrifice — then the father must heroically make this sacrifice. Nobly he must hide his pain, even though he might wish he were "the lowly man who dares to weep," and not the king who must act like a king. And though the pain enters his breast in solitude, and only three people in the nation share his secret, soon the whole nation will share in his pain — but will also share in his deed: that for the good of the whole he was willing to sacrifice her, his daughter, the lovely young girl. "O breast! O fair cheeks, golden hair!" (line 687). And the daughter will move him with her tears, and the father will turn his face away, but the hero will raise the knife. — And when the news of it reaches the ancestral home, the beautiful girls of Greece will blush with enthusiasm; and if the daughter was a bride, her betrothed will not be angry but proud to share in the father's deed, because the girl belonged to him more tenderly than she belonged to her father.

When the brave judge who saved Israel in its hour of need binds God and himself, in one breath, by the same vow, then he must heroically turn the young girl's jubilation, his beloved daughter's joy, into sorrow, and all Israel will mourn with her for her virgin youth. But every free-born man will understand Jephthah, every stout-hearted woman will admire him, and every virgin in Israel will wish to act as his daughter did. For what good would it have done that Jephthah won the victory through his vow, if he did not keep it? Would the victory not then be taken from the people again?

When a son forgets his duty, when the state entrusts the father with the sword of judgment, when the laws demand the punishment from the father's hand, then the father must heroically forget that the guilty one is his son. Nobly he must hide his pain, but there will not be a single person in the nation, not even the son, who does not admire the father. And every time the laws of Rome are interpreted, it will be remembered that many interpreted them more learnedly, but none more gloriously, than Brutus.

But suppose that Agamemnon, while a favorable wind was carrying the fleet under full sail toward its goal, had sent that messenger to fetch Iphigenia in order to sacrifice her. Suppose that Jephthah, without being bound by any vow that decided the fate of the people, had said to his daughter: "Mourn your short youth for two months now, and then I will sacrifice you." Suppose that Brutus had had a righteous son and had still called the lictors to execute him. Who would have understood them? And if these three men, asked why they did it, had answered, "It is a test in which we are being tried" — would anyone have understood them better?

When Agamemnon, Jephthah and Brutus, at the decisive moment, heroically overcome the pain, have heroically lost what they love, and have only to carry out the deed outwardly, then there will never be a noble soul in the world who does not shed tears of sympathy for their pain and tears of admiration for their deed. But suppose that at the decisive moment these three men were to add, to the heroism with which they bore the pain, these few little words: "But it will not happen." Who would understand them then? And if they added by way of explanation, "We believe this by virtue of the absurd," who would understand them any better? For who would not easily understand that it was absurd? But who would understand that one could then believe it?

The difference between the tragic hero and Abraham is plain to see. The tragic hero still stays within the ethical. He lets one expression of the ethical have its telos in a higher expression of the ethical. He reduces the ethical relation between father and son, or between daughter and father, to a feeling that has its dialectic in its relation to the idea of ethical life — a feeling, that is, that is weighed against that higher idea. So here there can be no question of a teleological suspension of the ethical itself.

With Abraham it is different. By his deed he overstepped the ethical altogether, and he had a higher telos outside it, in relation to which he suspended the ethical. For I would really like to know how anyone would bring Abraham's deed into relation with the universal — whether any connection whatever can be found between what Abraham did and the universal, other than that Abraham transgressed it. Abraham does not do it to save a nation, nor to uphold the idea of the state, nor to appease angry gods. If there could be any question of the deity being angry, he was angry only with Abraham, and Abraham's whole deed stands in no relation to the universal; it is a purely private undertaking. So while the tragic hero is great through the virtue of ethical life, Abraham is great through a purely personal virtue. In Abraham's life there is no higher expression of the ethical than this: the father must love the son. The ethical in the sense of ethical life is entirely out of the question here. Insofar as the universal was present at all, it was hidden in Isaac — concealed, so to speak, in Isaac's loins — and would have had to cry out with Isaac's mouth: "Do not do it! You are destroying everything."

Why, then, does Abraham do it? For God's sake — and, in complete identity with that, for his own sake. He does it for God's sake because God demands this proof of his faith; he does it for his own sake so that he can give the proof. The unity of these two is expressed quite correctly in the word that has always been used for this situation: it is a test, a temptation. A temptation — but what does that mean? What ordinarily tempts a person is whatever would hold him back from doing his duty. But here the temptation is the ethical itself, which would hold him back from doing God's will. What, then, is duty? Duty is, after all, precisely the expression of God's will.

Here it becomes clear that a new category is needed in order to understand Abraham. Paganism does not know such a relation to the deity. The tragic hero does not enter into any private relation to the deity; for him the ethical is the divine, and therefore the paradox in his situation can be mediated in the universal.

Abraham cannot be mediated — which can also be put this way: he cannot speak. As soon as I speak, I express the universal; and if I do not, no one can understand me. So as soon as Abraham wants to express himself in the universal, he has to say that his situation is a spiritual trial. For he has no higher expression of the universal that ranks above the universal he is transgressing.

So while Abraham arouses my admiration, he also appalls me. The person who denies himself and sacrifices himself for duty gives up the finite in order to grasp the infinite; he is secure enough. The tragic hero gives up what is certain for what is still more certain, and the onlooker's eye rests on him with confidence. But the one who gives up the universal to grasp something still higher that is not the universal — what is he doing? Is it possible that this could be anything other than a spiritual trial? And if it is possible, but the single individual was mistaken, what salvation is there for him? He suffers all the pain of the tragic hero, he destroys his joy in the world, he renounces everything — and perhaps at the same moment he bars himself from the exalted joy that was so precious to him that he would have bought it at any price. The onlooker cannot understand him at all, nor let his eye rest on him with confidence. Perhaps what the believer intends cannot be done at all, since it is unthinkable. Or if it could be done, but the single individual had misunderstood the deity, what salvation would there be for him then? The tragic hero needs tears and demands tears. And where was the envious eye so barren that it could not weep with Agamemnon? But where was the person whose soul was so lost that he presumed to weep over Abraham? The tragic hero completes his deed at a definite moment in time; but as time goes on he does something no less: he visits the person whose soul is gripped by sorrow, whose chest cannot draw breath for stifled sighs, whose thoughts hang heavy over him, pregnant with tears. He appears to him, breaks the spell of sorrow, loosens the corset, and draws out the tear, as the sufferer forgets his own sufferings in the hero's. Over Abraham no one can weep. One approaches him with a horror religiosus — a holy dread — as Israel approached Mount Sinai. — Suppose, then, that the solitary man who climbs Mount Moriah, whose peak towers sky-high above the plains of Aulis — suppose he is not a sleepwalker who walks safely over the abyss while the one who stands at the foot of the mountain, looking up, trembles with anxiety and, out of reverence and dread, does not even dare to call out to him — suppose he becomes confused in himself, suppose he had made a mistake! — Thanks, and thanks again, to the man who holds out to someone whom life's sorrows have assaulted and left naked the expression, the fig leaf of the word, with which he can cover his misery! Thanks to you, great Shakespeare, you who can say everything, everything, everything exactly as it is — and yet why did you never give voice to this torment? Did you perhaps keep it for yourself, like the beloved whose name one cannot even bear to hear the world speak? For a poet buys this power of the word, the power to speak all the heavy secrets of others, at the price of one little secret he cannot speak; and a poet is not an apostle — he casts out devils only by the power of the devil.

But when the ethical has been teleologically suspended in this way, how does the single individual in whom it is suspended exist? He exists as the single individual in opposition to the universal. Does he sin, then? For this is the form of sin, seen in terms of the idea (that is, in principle) — in such a way that even though a child does not sin, because it is not conscious of its existence as such, its existence is nevertheless sin when seen in terms of the idea, and the ethical demands itself of the child at every moment. If one denies that this form can be repeated in such a way that it is not sin, then judgment has been passed on Abraham. How, then, did Abraham exist? He had faith. This is the paradox that keeps him at the summit, the paradox he cannot make clear to anyone else. For the paradox is that he, as the single individual, puts himself in an absolute relation to the absolute. Is he justified? His justification is, once again, the paradox; for if he is justified, he is so not by virtue of being something universal but by virtue of being the single individual.

How, then, does the single individual make sure that he is justified? It is easy enough to level all of existence down to the idea of the state or the idea of society. If one does that, one can also mediate easily enough; for then one never arrives at the paradox that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — which I can also express pointedly with a saying of Pythagoras: that the odd number is more perfect than the even. Now and then in our time one does hear an answer that points in the direction of the paradox.

When one does, it usually runs like this: "It must be judged by the outcome." A hero who has become a skandalon — a stumbling block, an offense — to his contemporaries, conscious that he is a paradox who cannot make himself understood, calls out confidently to his age: "The outcome will surely prove that I was justified." In our time one hears this cry more rarely; for just as our age does not produce heroes, which is its failing, it has the advantage that it produces few caricatures either. So when in our time one hears the words "It must be judged by the outcome," one knows at once whom one has the honor of addressing. Those who talk this way are a numerous tribe, which I will call by the common name of the lecturers. In their thoughts they live secure in existence: they have a fixed position and safe prospects in a well-organized state; they have centuries, perhaps even millennia, between themselves and the upheavals of existence; they have no fear that such things could happen again — what would the police and the newspapers say? Their work in life is to judge the great men, and to judge them by the outcome. Such conduct toward greatness betrays a strange mixture of arrogance and wretchedness: arrogance, because they think themselves called to judge; wretchedness, because they do not feel their own lives to be even remotely related to those of the great. Anyone with even a little erectioris ingenii — a more elevated cast of mind — has not become an entirely cold and clammy mollusk; and as he approaches what is great, he can never forget that since the creation of the world it has been the custom for the outcome to come last, and that if one is truly to learn anything from what is great, one must pay attention precisely to the beginning. If the one who is to act wants to judge himself by the outcome, he will never begin. Even if the outcome delights the whole world, it cannot help the hero; for he learned the outcome only when the whole thing was over, and it was not by the outcome that he became a hero — he was one because he began.

Besides, the outcome (insofar as it is finitude's answer to the infinite question) is, in its dialectic — in the way it works — entirely different in kind from the hero's existence. Or is the fact that Abraham received Isaac by a miracle supposed to prove that Abraham was justified in relating himself as the single individual to the universal? If Abraham had actually sacrificed Isaac, would he have been any less justified?

But people are curious about the outcome, as they are about how a book ends. The anxiety, the distress, the paradox — of these they want to know nothing. They flirt aesthetically with the outcome; it arrives just as unexpectedly, but also just as easily, as a lottery prize; and once they have heard the outcome, they feel edified. And yet no temple robber laboring in chains and irons is so base a criminal as the one who plunders the holy in this way; and not even Judas, who sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver, is more contemptible than the one who sells greatness in this way.

It goes against my soul to speak inhumanly about greatness — to let it loom dimly, in vague outline, at an enormous distance; to let it be great without bringing out what is human in it, whereupon it ceases to be great. For it is not what happens to me that makes me great, but what I do; and surely no one thinks a man became great because he won the big prize in the lottery. Even if a person was born in humble circumstances, I still require of him that he not be so inhuman toward himself that he can think of the king's castle only from a distance, dreaming vaguely of its greatness, at once wanting to exalt it and abolishing it by exalting it in a servile way. I require of him that he be human enough to step forward there too, with confidence and dignity. He must not be so inhuman as to want to violate everything impudently by storming straight in from the street into the king's halls; by doing so he loses more than the king does. On the contrary, he should find joy in observing every rule of propriety with a glad and confident enthusiasm, which is exactly what will make him free and bold. This is only an image, for that difference in rank is a very imperfect expression of distance in the world of spirit. I require of every human being that he not think so inhumanly of himself that he does not dare to enter those palaces where not only the memory of the chosen lives but where the chosen themselves live. He should not push forward impudently and force his kinship on them. He should be blessed every time he bows before them, but he should be bold and confident, and always something more than a charwoman; for if he will not be more than that, he will never get in. And what will help him is precisely the anxiety and distress in which the great are tested; for otherwise, if he has any backbone at all, the great would only arouse his justified envy. And whatever can be great only at a distance, whatever people try to make great with empty and hollow phrases — that they destroy themselves.

Who was ever as great in the world as that favored woman, the Mother of God, the Virgin Mary? And yet how do people speak of her? That she was the favored one among women does not make her great. And if it did not so strangely happen that those who listen can think just as inhumanly as those who speak, then surely every young girl would ask: "Why was I not the favored one too?" And if I had nothing else to say, I would certainly not dismiss such a question as stupid; for when it comes to a favor, seen abstractly, every human being has an equal claim. What people leave out is the distress, the anxiety, the paradox. My thought is as pure as anyone's, and whoever can think such things will surely find his thought becoming pure; and if it does not, he has something terrible to expect. For whoever has once called up these images cannot get rid of them again.

And if he sins against them, they take revenge terribly, with a silent wrath more terrible than the loud clamor of ten ravening reviewers. Mary did bear the child miraculously, but it went with her as it goes with women, and that time is a time of anxiety, distress and paradox. The angel was indeed a ministering spirit, but he was not an obliging spirit who went around to the other young girls in Israel and said, "Do not despise Mary; something extraordinary is happening to her." The angel came only to Mary, and no one could understand her. What woman was ever so humiliated as Mary? And is it not true here as well that the one whom God blesses he curses in the same breath? This is how the spirit understands Mary. And she is by no means — it outrages me to say it, but it outrages me even more that people have thoughtlessly and frivolously thought of her this way — she is by no means a fine lady sitting in state and playing with a divine child. When, despite all this, she said, "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord," then she is great; and I think it will not be hard to explain why she became the Mother of God. She needs no worldly admiration, any more than Abraham needs tears; for she was no heroine, and he was no hero. But both of them became greater than heroes — not at all by being spared the distress, the torment and the paradox, but through them.

It is great when the poet, presenting his tragic hero for people's admiration, dares to say: "Weep for him, for he deserves it." For it is great to deserve the tears of those who deserve to shed tears. It is great that the poet dares to hold the crowd in check, dares to discipline people, so that each one examines himself to see whether he is worthy to weep over the hero; for the waste water of blubberers degrades what is holy. — But greater than all this is that the knight of faith dares to say even to the noble person who wants to weep over him: "Do not weep for me, but weep for yourself."

People are moved; they long to go back to those beautiful times; sweet, tender longings lead them to the goal of their wish — to see Christ walking about in the promised land. They forget the anxiety, the distress, the paradox. Was it such an easy matter not to be mistaken? Was it not terrifying that this man who walked among the others was God? Was it not terrifying to sit at table with him? Was it such an easy matter to become an apostle? But the outcome, eighteen centuries, helps — it helps with this shabby deception by which people deceive themselves and others. I do not feel courageous enough to wish I had been contemporary with such events; but for that reason I do not judge harshly those who were mistaken, nor think little of those who saw what was right.
But I return to Abraham. In the time before the outcome, either Abraham was a murderer every minute, or we stand before the paradox that is higher than all mediations.

The story of Abraham, then, contains a teleological suspension of the ethical. As the single individual, he has become higher than the universal. This is the paradox that cannot be mediated. It is just as inexplicable how he entered it as how he remains in it. If this is not how things stand with Abraham, then he is not even a tragic hero but a murderer. To go on calling him the father of faith, to talk about this to people who care about nothing but words, is thoughtless. A human being can become a tragic hero by his own strength, but not a knight of faith. When someone sets out on the tragic hero's road — hard, in a certain sense — many will be able to advise him; but the one who walks the narrow road of faith no one can advise, no one can understand.
Faith is a miracle, and yet no human being is excluded from it; for what unites all human life is passion, and faith is a passion.*

notes.text: * Lessing once said something similar from a purely aesthetic standpoint. What he actually wants to show in that passage is that grief, too, can find witty expression. To that end he quotes a remark made in a particular situation by the unhappy English king Edward II. In contrast to this, he cites, following Diderot, a story about a peasant woman and a remark of hers. He then continues: "Auch das war Witz, und noch dazu Witz einer Bäuerin; aber die Umstände machten ihn unvermeidlich. Und folglich auch muss man die Entschuldigung der witzigen Ausdrücke des Schmerzes und der Betrübniss nicht darin suchen, dass die Person, welche sie sagt, eine vornehme, wohlerzogene, verständige, und auch sonst witzige Person sey; denn die Leidenschaften machen alle Menschen wieder gleich: sondern darin, dass wahrscheinlicher Weise ein jeder Mensch ohne Unterschied in den nämlichen Umständen das nämliche sagen würde. Den Gedanken der Bäuerin hätte eine Königin haben können und haben müssen: so wie das, was dort der König sagt, auch ein Bauer hätte sagen können und ohne Zweifel würde gesagt haben." [That too was wit, and a peasant woman's wit at that; but the circumstances made it unavoidable. And consequently the excuse for witty expressions of pain and grief must not be sought in the fact that the person who says them is a distinguished, well-bred, intelligent and otherwise witty person; for the passions make all human beings equal again. It must be sought in the fact that, in all probability, every human being without distinction would say the same thing in the same circumstances. A queen could have had, and must have had, the peasant woman's thought, just as what the king says there a peasant too could have said, and no doubt would have said.] Cf. Sämtliche Werke, vol. 30, p. 293.

chapters.title: Problema II — Is there an absolute duty to God?
paragraphs: The ethical is the universal, and as such it is also the divine. So it is right to say that every duty is at bottom a duty to God. But if one can say no more than that, then one is also saying that I really have no duty to God. A duty becomes a duty by being referred to God, but in the duty itself I do not enter into a relation with God. Thus it is a duty to love one's neighbor. It is a duty because it is referred to God; but in this duty I enter into a relation not with God but with the neighbor I love. If I then say, in this context, that it is my duty to love God, I am really saying only a tautology — the same thing twice — insofar as "God" is here taken in a wholly abstract sense as the divine, that is, the universal, that is, duty. The whole existence of the human race is then rounded off in itself, complete as a sphere, and the ethical is at once what bounds it and what fills it. God becomes an invisible, vanishing point, a powerless thought; his power is only in the ethical, which fills all of existence. So if anyone should take it into his head to love God in any sense other than the one just stated, he is overwrought: he loves a phantom which, if it only had strength enough to speak, would say to him, "I do not ask for your love; just stay where you belong." If anyone should take it into his head to love God in some other way, this love becomes suspect, like the love Rousseau speaks of, with which a person loves a far-off African people instead of loving his neighbor.

Now, if what has been set out here is correct — if there is nothing incommensurable in a human life, and whatever incommensurable there is exists only by accident, from which nothing follows insofar as existence is viewed in terms of the idea — then Hegel is right. But where he is not right is in speaking of faith, or in allowing Abraham to be regarded as its father; for by the latter he has pronounced judgment on both Abraham and faith. In Hegel's philosophy, das Äussere (die Entäusserung) — the outer (the act of outwardly expressing oneself) — is higher than das Innere, the inner. This is often illustrated with an example. The child is das Innere, the man das Äussere; that is why the child is determined precisely by what is outer, and, conversely, why the man, as das Äussere, is determined precisely by das Innere. Faith, however, is this paradox: that inwardness is higher than outwardness — or, to recall an expression used earlier, that the odd number is higher than the even.

For the ethical view of life, then, the task of the single individual is to strip himself of the determination of inwardness and to express it in something outward. Every time the single individual shrinks from this, every time he wants to hold back in, or slip back into, the inward determinations of feeling, mood and so on, he sins; he is in a spiritual trial. The paradox of faith is this: that there is an inwardness that is incommensurable with the outward — an inwardness which, note carefully, is not identical with the first inwardness but is a new inwardness.

This must not be overlooked. Recent philosophy has allowed itself, without further ado, to substitute "the immediate" — what is simply there before any reflection — for "faith." If one does that, it is ridiculous to deny that faith has existed in every age. Faith then ends up in rather common company, alongside feeling, mood, idiosyncrasy, vapeurs (fits of the vapors) and so on. To that extent philosophy may be right that one ought not to stop there. But nothing justifies philosophy in using language this way. Faith is preceded by a movement of infinity; only then does faith appear, nec opinate — unexpectedly — by virtue of the absurd. This I can well understand, without thereby claiming that I have faith. If faith is nothing more than what philosophy passes it off as, then Socrates already went further, much further — instead of the reverse, that he did not reach it. In an intellectual respect he made the movement of infinity. His ignorance is infinite resignation. That task is in itself one suited to human strength, even if our age disdains it. But only when it has been done, only when the single individual has exhausted himself in the infinite, only then has the point been reached where faith can break through.

The paradox of faith, then, is this: that the single individual is higher than the universal; that the single individual — to recall a theological distinction now less often heard — determines his relation to the universal by his relation to the absolute, not his relation to the absolute by his relation to the universal. The paradox can also be put this way: there is an absolute duty to God. For in this relation of duty the single individual, as the single individual, relates himself absolutely to the absolute. So when it is said in this connection that it is a duty to love God, something different is being said from before. For if this duty is absolute, then the ethical is reduced to the relative. It does not follow that the ethical is to be abolished; rather, it receives an entirely different expression, the paradoxical expression — so that, for example, love for God can lead the knight of faith to give his love for his neighbor an expression that is the opposite of what, ethically speaking, is his duty.
If this is not so, then faith has no place in existence; then faith is a spiritual trial, and Abraham is lost, since he gave in to it.

This paradox cannot be mediated, for it rests precisely on the single individual's being only the single individual. As soon as this single individual wants to express his absolute duty in the universal and become conscious of it there, he recognizes that he is in a spiritual trial. And then, if he does resist it, he will not come to fulfill the so-called absolute duty; and if he does not resist it, he sins, even if in reality his deed turns out to be what was his absolute duty. So what was Abraham to do? If he had said to another person, "I love Isaac more than anything in the world, and that is why it is so hard for me to sacrifice him," the other would surely have shaken his head and said, "Then why sacrifice him?" Or, if the other had been a shrewd fellow, he might even have seen through Abraham and noticed that he was displaying feelings that flagrantly contradicted his deed.

In the story of Abraham we find just such a paradox. Ethically expressed, his relation to Isaac is this: the father must love the son. This ethical relation is reduced to the relative, in contrast to the absolute relation to God. To the question "Why?" Abraham has no answer except that it is a test, a temptation — which, as noted above, is the unity of its being for God's sake and for his own sake. These two determinations also correspond to each other in ordinary speech. When we see someone do something that does not fit into the universal, we say, "He hardly did that for God's sake," and by this we mean that he did it for his own sake. The paradox of faith has lost the intermediate term, that is, the universal. On the one side it has the expression of the most extreme egoism (doing the terrible thing it does for its own sake); on the other side, the expression of the most absolute devotion (doing it for God's sake). Faith itself cannot be mediated into the universal, for that would cancel it. Faith is this paradox, and the single individual simply cannot make himself understood by anyone. People imagine that the single individual can make himself understood by another single individual who is in the same position. Such a view would be unthinkable if people in our time were not trying in so many ways to sneak slyly into greatness. One knight of faith cannot help another at all. Either the single individual becomes a knight of faith himself, by taking the paradox upon himself, or he never becomes one. Partnership in these regions is utterly unthinkable. Any more precise explanation of what is to be understood by "Isaac" the single individual can only ever give to himself. And even if one could define ever so exactly, in general terms, what is to be understood by "Isaac" (which, incidentally, would be the most ridiculous self-contradiction: bringing the single individual, who stands precisely outside the universal, under universal definitions, when he is supposed to act precisely as the single individual who is outside the universal), the single individual could still never be assured of it by others, only by himself as the single individual. So even if a person were cowardly and wretched enough to want to become a knight of faith on someone else's responsibility, he would not become one; for only the single individual becomes one, as the single individual. And that is what is great — which I can understand without entering into it, since I lack the courage. But it is also what is terrible — which I can grasp even better.

As is well known, Luke 14:26 sets out a remarkable teaching about the absolute duty to God: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters — yes, even his own life — he cannot be my disciple." This is a hard saying; who can bear to hear it? For that reason it is heard very seldom. But this silence is only an evasion, and it does no good. The student of theology, meanwhile, learns that these words occur in the New Testament, and in some exegetical handbook he finds the information that μισεῖν (to hate), in this and a few other passages, is used per μείωσιν — by understatement — and means minus diligo, posthabeo, non colo, nihili facio: I love less, I put in second place, I do not honor, I count as nothing. The context in which these words occur, however, does not seem to support this tasteful explanation. For the very next verse tells how someone who wants to build a tower first calculates whether he is able to finish it, so that people will not laugh at him afterward. The close connection between this story and the verse quoted seems to indicate precisely that the words are to be taken as terribly as possible, so that each person may examine himself to see whether he can put up the building.

Suppose that pious and tender-minded exegete, who thinks he can smuggle Christianity into the world by haggling it down in this way, managed to convince someone that this was — grammatically, linguistically and κατ' ἀναλογίαν (by analogy with other passages) — the meaning of that passage. Then he will hopefully also manage, in the same moment, to convince that same person that Christianity is one of the most pitiful things in the world. For consider a teaching that, in one of its most lyrical outbursts, where the consciousness of its eternal validity swells most powerfully within it, has nothing to say but a noisy word that means nothing and indicates only that one should be less kind, less attentive, more indifferent; a teaching that, at the very moment it makes as if to say something terrible, ends by soothing instead of terrifying — that teaching is surely not worth standing up for.

The words are terrible, yet I do believe they can be understood — without it following that whoever has understood them therefore has the courage to do what they say. One should at least be honest enough to acknowledge what is written there, and to admit that it is great, even if one lacks the courage for it oneself. Whoever behaves this way will not shut himself out from a share in that beautiful story; for in a way it contains comfort even for the one who did not have the courage to begin building the tower. But he must be honest, and not pass off this lack of courage as humility; for, on the contrary, it is pride, whereas the courage of faith is the only humble courage.

It is easy to see now that if the passage is to make any sense, it must be understood literally. God is the one who demands absolute love. Now, anyone who demands a person's love and thinks that this love should also prove itself by the person's becoming lukewarm toward everything else he held dear is not only an egoist but also stupid. And whoever demanded such a love would at the same moment be signing his own death sentence, insofar as his life lay in the love he desired. A husband, for example, requires his wife to leave father and mother. But if he were to regard it as proof of her extraordinary love for him that for his sake she became a lukewarm, listless daughter, and so on, then he is stupider than the stupidest. If he had any idea of what love is, he would wish to discover that she was perfect in love as a daughter and a sister.
In that he would see a guarantee that his wife would love him as no one else in the kingdom could.
So: what one would regard in a human being as a sign of egoism and stupidity —
that, with the help of an exegete, one is supposed to regard as a worthy conception of the deity.

But how, then, is one to hate them? I will not bring up here the human distinction "either love or hate" — not because I have much against it, for it is at least passionate, but because it is egoistic and does not fit here. If, however, I regard the task as a paradox, then I understand it — that is, I understand it in the way one can understand a paradox. The absolute duty can then lead one to do what ethics would forbid, but it can by no means lead the knight of faith to stop loving. Abraham shows this. At the moment he is about to sacrifice Isaac, the ethical expression for what he is doing is this: he hates Isaac. But if he really hates Isaac, he can rest assured that God does not require this of him; for Cain and Abraham are not the same. Isaac he must love with his whole soul. When God demands Isaac, Abraham must love him, if possible, even more — and only then can he sacrifice him. For it is precisely this love for Isaac that, by its paradoxical opposition to his love for God, makes his deed a sacrifice. But the distress and anxiety in the paradox is that, humanly speaking, he cannot make himself understood at all. Only at the moment when his deed is in absolute contradiction to his feeling does he sacrifice Isaac. But the reality of his deed is what makes him belong to the universal, and there he is and remains a murderer.

The passage in Luke must further be understood in such a way that one sees that the knight of faith has no higher expression of the universal (in the sense of the ethical) in which he could save himself. If, for example, the Church were to demand this sacrifice of one of its members, we would have only a tragic hero. For the idea of the Church is not qualitatively different from the idea of the state, as long as the single individual can enter it by a simple mediation.

And as soon as the single individual has entered the paradox, he does not arrive at the idea of the Church; he does not get out of the paradox, but must find in it either his blessedness or his perdition. Such an ecclesiastical hero expresses the universal in his deed, and there will be no one in the Church — not even his father and mother, and so on — who does not understand him. But he is not a knight of faith, and he also gives a different answer from Abraham's: he does not say that it is a test or a temptation in which he is being tried.

People generally refrain from quoting passages like this one in Luke. They are afraid of letting people loose; they fear the worst will happen once the single individual takes it into his head to behave as the single individual. Moreover, people think that existing as the single individual is the easiest thing of all, and that this is exactly why people must be forced to become the universal. I can share neither that fear nor that opinion, and for the same reason. Whoever has learned that existing as the single individual is the most terrible thing of all will not be afraid to say that it is the greatest. But he must also say it in such a way that his words hardly become a snare for someone who has gone astray, but rather help him into the universal — even if his words make a little room for what is great. Whoever does not dare to mention such passages does not dare to mention Abraham either. And to think that existing as the single individual is easy enough contains a very dubious indirect admission about oneself. For whoever really has self-respect and concern for his soul is certain that the one who lives under his own supervision, alone in the whole world, lives more strictly and more chastely than a maiden in her chamber. It is true that there may be those who need compulsion — those who, if they were set free, would romp like unruly animals in selfish pleasure. But one must show that one is not one of them precisely by knowing how to speak with anxiety and trembling. And one should speak out of reverence for what is great, so that it is not forgotten out of fear of harm — harm that will surely not come if one speaks in such a way that one knows it is the great, knows its terrors; and without knowing those, one does not know its greatness either.

Let us now consider the distress and anxiety in the paradox of faith a little more closely. The tragic hero renounces himself in order to express the universal; the knight of faith renounces the universal in order to become the single individual. As was said, everything depends on how one is placed. Whoever thinks it is easy enough to be the single individual can always be sure that he is not a knight of faith; for drifters and vagabond geniuses are not men of faith. The knight of faith, on the contrary, knows that it is glorious to belong to the universal. He knows it is beautiful and beneficial to be the single individual who translates himself into the universal — who, so to speak, himself produces a clean, elegant and as far as possible error-free edition of himself, legible to all. He knows it is refreshing to become understandable to himself in the universal, in such a way that he understands it, and that every single individual who understands him in turn understands the universal in him, and both rejoice in the security of the universal. He knows it is beautiful to be born as the single individual who has his home in the universal, his friendly dwelling place, which at once receives him with open arms whenever he wants to stay in it. But he also knows that higher up than this there winds a lonely path, narrow and steep. He knows it is terrible to be born in solitude out of the universal, to walk without meeting a single traveler. He knows very well where he is and how he stands in relation to other people. Humanly speaking, he is mad and cannot make himself understood by anyone. And yet "mad" is the mildest expression. If he is not regarded that way, then he is a hypocrite — and the higher he climbs on that path, the more dreadful a hypocrite he is.

The knight of faith knows that it is inspiring to give oneself up for the universal, that it takes courage, but also that there is a security in it, precisely because it is for the universal. He knows that it is glorious to be understood by every noble mind, and in such a way that the onlooker himself is ennobled by it. This he knows, and he feels as if bound; he could wish that this were the task that had been set for him. So Abraham might now and then have wished that the task were to love Isaac as befits a father, understandably to all, memorably for all time; he could wish that the task were to sacrifice Isaac for the universal, so that he could inspire fathers to glorious deeds. And he is almost horrified at the thought that for him such wishes are only spiritual trials and must be treated as such; for he knows that it is a lonely path he walks, and that he accomplishes nothing for the universal but is himself only tried and tested. Or what did Abraham accomplish for the universal? Let me speak humanly about it, really humanly! He spends seventy years getting a son in his old age. What others get quickly enough and enjoy for a long time takes him seventy years. And why? Because he is being tested and tempted. Is that not madness? But Abraham had faith, and only Sarah wavered and got him to take Hagar as a concubine — but for that reason he also had to drive Hagar away. He gets Isaac — and then he is to be tested again. He knew it is glorious to express the universal, glorious to live with Isaac. But that is not the task. He knew it is kingly to sacrifice such a son for the universal; he himself would have found rest in it, and everyone would have rested in praise of his deed, as a vowel rests in the silent letter that carries it. But that is not the task — he is being tested. There was a Roman general famous by the surname Cunctator, "the Delayer."

He stopped the enemy by delaying — but what a delayer Abraham is compared with him! Yet Abraham does not save the state. This is the content of 130 years. Who can bear it? Would his contemporaries — if one could speak of his having any — not say: "With Abraham it is an eternal delaying. At last he got a son — it took long enough — and now he wants to sacrifice him. Is he not out of his mind? If only he could at least explain why he wants to do it; but it is always 'a test.'" Nor could Abraham explain any more than that; for his life is like a book that has been placed under divine seizure and never becomes publici juris — public property.

This is what is terrible. Whoever does not see it can always be sure that he is no knight of faith. But whoever does see it will not want to deny that even the most sorely tried tragic hero moves as if in a dance compared with the knight of faith, who makes his way forward only slowly, crawling. And when he has seen this and has made sure that he lacks the courage to understand it, he will surely have some sense of the wondrous glory that knight attains: he becomes God's confidant, the Lord's friend — to speak quite humanly — so that he speaks to God in heaven as one speaks to an intimate, saying "you," while even the tragic hero addresses him only in the third person.

The tragic hero is soon finished, and his struggle is soon over. He makes the infinite movement and is now secure in the universal. The knight of faith, on the other hand, is kept sleepless; for he is constantly being tested, and at every moment there is the possibility of turning back in repentance to the universal — and this possibility can just as well be a spiritual trial as the truth. He cannot get clarity about this from any human being; for then he would be outside the paradox.

The knight of faith, then, has first and foremost the passion to concentrate the whole of the ethical that he is breaking into a single moment, so that he can assure himself that he really loves Isaac with his whole soul.* If he cannot do that, he is in a spiritual trial. Next, he has the passion to call up this whole assurance in an instant, and in such a way that it is just as fully valid as it was in the first moment. If he cannot do that, he gets nowhere; for then he must keep starting over from the beginning. The tragic hero also concentrates into one moment the ethical that he teleologically went beyond, but in this respect he has support in the universal. The knight of faith has only himself alone, and that is what is terrible. Most people live in an ethical obligation in such a way that they let each day have its own sorrow; but then they never arrive at this passionate concentration, this energetic consciousness. In a certain sense the universal can help the tragic hero attain it, but the knight of faith is alone in everything.

The tragic hero does it and finds rest in the universal; the knight of faith is kept in constant tension. Agamemnon gives up Iphigenia and has thereby found rest in the universal; now he proceeds to sacrifice her. If Agamemnon has not made the movement — if at the decisive moment his soul, instead of passionate concentration, was lost in the common chatter about having several daughters and about how vielleicht das Ausserordentliche (perhaps the extraordinary) might still happen — then of course he is no hero but a case for the poorhouse. Abraham has the hero's concentration too, though in him it is far more difficult, since he has no support at all in the universal; but he makes one more movement, by which he gathers his soul back upon the miracle. If Abraham has not done that, he is only an Agamemnon — assuming one could even explain how it can be justified to want to sacrifice Isaac when doing so benefits the universal in no way.

Whether the single individual is really in a spiritual trial or is a knight of faith, only the single individual himself can decide. Nevertheless, some marks can be constructed from the paradox that even someone who is not in it can understand. The true knight of faith is always absolute isolation; the false knight is sectarian. Sectarianism is an attempt to jump off the narrow path of the paradox and become a tragic hero on the cheap. The tragic hero expresses the universal and sacrifices himself for it. Instead of this, the sectarian Master Jackel — a puppet-show clown — has a private theater, a few good friends and comrades who represent the universal about as well as the court witnesses in The Gold Snuffbox represent justice. The knight of faith, on the contrary, is the paradox; he is the single individual, absolutely nothing but the single individual, without any connections or complications. This is the terrible thing that the sectarian weakling cannot endure. For instead of learning from it that he is unable to do what is great, and then plainly admitting it — something I naturally cannot but approve of, since it is what I do myself — the bungler thinks that by joining forces with a few other bunglers he will be able to do it. But that will not work at all; in the world of spirit no cheating is tolerated. A dozen sectarians go arm in arm; they know nothing at all of the lonely spiritual trials that await the knight of faith and that he dares not flee, precisely because it would be still more terrible if he presumptuously forced his way forward. The sectarians drown one another out with noise and clamor and keep anxiety away with their shouting; and a hooting fairground crowd like this thinks it is storming heaven and thinks it is walking the same path as the knight of faith — who, in the solitude of the universe, never hears a human voice but walks alone with his terrible responsibility.

The knight of faith is thrown back on himself alone. He feels the pain of not being able to make himself understood by others, but he feels no vain desire to guide others. The pain is his assurance. The vain desire he does not know; his soul is too earnest for that. The false knight easily betrays himself by the mastery he has acquired in an instant. He does not grasp at all what is at issue: that if another single individual is to walk the same path, he must become the single individual in exactly the same way, and then he needs no one's guidance — least of all from someone who wants to force it on him. Here, again, people jump off the path: they cannot endure the martyrdom of being uncomprehended, and instead, conveniently enough, they choose the worldly admiration that mastery brings. The true knight of faith is a witness, never a teacher, and in this lies the deep humanity that is worth far more than the silly concern for other people's weal and woe that is honored under the name of sympathy, though it is nothing but vanity. Whoever wants only to be a witness thereby confesses that no human being, not even the lowliest, needs another's sympathy or should be humbled by it so that the other can be raised up. But just as he did not win what he won on the cheap, he does not sell it cheap either. He is not base enough to accept people's admiration and pay them for it with his silent contempt. He knows that what is truly great is equally accessible to all.

So either there is an absolute duty to God — and if there is, it is the paradox described here: that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal and as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute — or else there has never been faith, because it has always existed; or else Abraham is lost; or else one must explain the passage in Luke 14 as that tasteful exegete did, and explain the corresponding passages, and similar ones, in the same way.

notes.text: * I want to shed light once more on the difference between the collision as it confronts the tragic hero and as it confronts the knight of faith. The tragic hero assures himself that the ethical obligation is wholly present in him by transforming it into a wish. Agamemnon can thus say: "The proof, for me, that I am not violating my duty as a father is that what is my duty is my only wish." So here we have wish and duty facing each other. The happy thing in life is when the two coincide, when my wish is my duty and vice versa, and most people's task in life is precisely to remain in their duty and, by their enthusiasm, to transform it into their wish. The tragic hero gives up his wish in order to fulfill his duty. For the knight of faith, too, wish and duty are identical, but he is required to give up both. So if he wants to resign himself by giving up his wish, he finds no rest; for it is, after all, his duty. If he wants to remain in his duty and in his wish, he does not become the knight of faith; for the absolute duty required precisely that he give it up. The tragic hero received a higher expression of duty, but not an absolute duty.
